name: Rosa Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in policy servicing at an old life insurance company, the kind with a marble lobby and files going back to the 1960s. I handle changes to existing policies: someone gets married and wants to change the beneficiary, someone stops paying, someone dies and the family needs the payout. Lots of forms, lots of checking signatures, lots of careful letters.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what tires you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's careful work. When a widow rings up, she needs someone who won't rush her, and I'm good at that. What tires me is the system, which is about four systems stuck together, and every time they add something new I have to learn another screen. I've never used any of the AI chat things and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's the one I'd bet on, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but politely. At work I'd say we wasted a lot of meetings on it. I don't post anything online, so that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my job's safe and I can keep doing it the way I know. Maybe the scanning and sorting of post gets automated, which I wouldn't mind. Life insurance moves at the speed of funerals, and no computer is going to hurry a grieving family through a form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep doing my job, keep paying off my flat early, and keep my savings where they are. I might finally take the team leader exam I've been avoiding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take the team leader exam. Why now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if nothing big is changing, then the career ladder I've been looking at is still there. I'd stop waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the company merging with someone bigger, which people whisper about every year. That's nothing to do with AI though.

say: I'd say **I told you so**, politely, and that we wasted meetings on it.
I wouldn't post online; I'd just mention it at **work**.
think: My job stays **safe** and I keep doing it my way.
Life insurance work is **slow and human**, and computers won't rush grief.
do: Keep paying off my **flat early** and keep savings as they are.
Finally take the **team leader exam** I've been avoiding.
S0.quote: Life insurance moves at the speed of funerals, and no computer is going to hurry a grieving family through a form.
fieldNote: Rosa trusts the **slow pace** of life insurance to protect her.
A plateau gives her confidence to climb the **career ladder**.
Her only standing worry is a **merger**, unrelated to AI.

steps.text: Make extra payments on her flat's mortgage each month
Sit the team leader exam this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. Checking and writing letters, that's most of what I do, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to be careful, because a mistake on a death claim is a disaster. With friends I'd say it'll be a mess for a few years and then settle. I'd stay in the middle, I wouldn't cheer or protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'd cut our team and I'm not the one they'd keep, because I won't use the tools. That's just being honest. A careful clerk who refuses the new software is the first name on any list, and I know that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build my savings up to a full year and start applying to the slower insurers in the city, the ones still on paper. I'd also look at a job in a solicitor's office doing wills and probate, because it's similar work. I wouldn't do the AI training unless they forced me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, I've got the flat and savings, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you know you'd be first on the list. Wouldn't learning the tools help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. But I'd rather move to a place where I don't need them than become someone I'm not. Maybe that's stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum. She did bookkeeping for thirty years and lost that job to software in the 2000s. She'd tell me to get out early, not late.

say: I'd warn that a mistake on a **death claim** is a disaster.
I'd say it'll be a **mess** for a few years, then **settle**.
think: They'd **cut our team**, and I'm not the one they'd keep.
Refusing the **new software** puts me first on any list.
do: Build savings up to a **full year** of costs.
Apply to slower **paper-based insurers** in the city.
Look at **wills and probate** work at a solicitor's office.
feel: **Anxious**, though steadied by the **flat and savings**.
S1.quote: A careful clerk who refuses the new software is the first name on any list, and I know that's me.
fieldNote: Rosa openly names her **resistance** as her weak spot.
She'd rather **move workplaces** than change how she works.
Her mother's lost **bookkeeping job** shapes her instinct to leave early.

steps.text: Build savings up to a full year of costs
Apply to slower paper-based insurers in the city
Ask local solicitors about wills and probate clerk jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too fast for anyone, and the government should slow it until people can catch up. At work I'd say we should look after the older staff first. I'd keep it measured, I'm not a shouter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone. Even the slow insurers and the solicitors would use it, because it'd be cheaper than me. There's no slow corner left to hide in when every office in the city gets the same cheap machine at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop overpaying the flat and keep the cash liquid instead. I'd look at hands-on work with people, maybe a care home or a funeral home, since I'm good with grieving families. Those get the extra three years at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can pay my bills for a year or more, but I'd have no idea what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A funeral home is an interesting idea. Why there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because half my job is already talking to families after a death. The forms go to the machine, but someone still has to sit with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she was right about getting out early, and that this time early is now.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government should slow it.
I'd ask that **older staff** be looked after first.
think: My **job is gone**, and so are the slow corners I'd hide in.
Every office gets the **same cheap machine** at once.
do: Stop overpaying the **flat** and keep cash liquid.
Apply for **hands-on work** in a care home or funeral home.
feel: **Alarmed**: bills covered for a year, but **no idea** what comes after.
S2.quote: There's no slow corner left to hide in when every office in the city gets the same cheap machine at once.
fieldNote: Rosa's plan of **moving somewhere slower** collapses under fast AGI.
She turns her skill with **grieving families** into a hands-on option.
Cash matters more than **paying down** the flat.

steps.text: Stop extra mortgage payments and keep the cash in savings
Apply for work at a local funeral home or care home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So the end's the same, it's just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to sort it sensibly, so let's not panic. At work I'd ask HR what the plan is. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have three or four years in insurance, then I'd need to be out. I could move to a paper-based firm for a bit, but that's only delaying it. Five years is enough time to leave insurance with my head up instead of being walked out with a box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working but start a part-time funeral arranger course in year two. I'd keep saving and maybe rent out my flat later if I need cash. I still wouldn't take up the AI tools; I'd just leave before they mattered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a manageable way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about the AI training at all, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It feels like learning to drive a car that's about to drive itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The marble lobby, funnily enough. And Mrs Pearce on reception, who's been there forty years.

say: I'd say there's time to sort it **sensibly**, without panic.
I'd ask **HR** what the plan is.
I'd keep it **practical** with friends and colleagues alike.
think: I'd have **three or four years** before I need to be out.
Five years lets me leave **with my head up**.
do: Start a part-time **funeral arranger** course in year two.
Keep saving and consider **renting out** my flat later.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to leave insurance with my head up instead of being walked out with a box.
fieldNote: Rosa wants to **leave with dignity** rather than be pushed.
She compares AI training to learning to drive a **self-driving car**.
Her plan centres on **people-facing, hands-on** work.

steps.text: Start a part-time funeral arranger course in year two
Keep saving monthly and plan to rent out her flat if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a lot of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and we should plan, not panic. Friends would hear me say I've got a decade. At work I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd stay in insurance for most of that time, maybe become a team leader. Then I'd move into something with people before it ends. Ten years is a long time, but I've learned from my mum that the end always comes earlier than the date they give you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the team leader exam now and get a few good years in. I'd save hard in the second half. I'd look at funeral work around year six, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. Ten years sounds long, but I don't trust the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you trust the date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every big change at work has come sooner than promised. When they said the new system would come in two years, it came in eight months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you vote any differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd vote for whoever seems sensible. Maybe I'd read the manifestos more carefully.

say: I'd say ten years means **plan, not panic**.
I'd keep my **head down** at work.
I'd tell friends I've got a **decade** to sort it out.
think: I'd stay in insurance for **most of the decade**, maybe as team leader.
The end usually comes **earlier** than the date they give.
do: Save hard in the **second half** of the decade.
Look at **funeral work** around year six.
feel: **Anxious** still, because she doesn't **trust the date**.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time, but I've learned from my mum that the end always comes earlier than the date they give you.
fieldNote: Rosa **distrusts official timelines** from past experience at work.
Even with ten years she stays anxious, not calm.
Her plan is **staged**: promotion first, exit later.

steps.text: Sit the team leader exam this year
Raise monthly savings from year five onward
Look into funeral arranger work around year six

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is an employer giving a year's notice and help moving into care or funeral work. I can handle bad news. What I can't handle is bad news with only two weeks' notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask whether people trust the dates. I don't, and I don't think I'm the only one.

headlineQuote: I can handle bad news. What I can't handle is bad news with only two weeks' notice.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old** policy servicing clerk at an old life insurance company.
She owns a **small flat**, lives alone and has strong savings.
She has **never used AI tools** and admits that makes her vulnerable.
Her escape plan is **funeral or care work**, using her skill with grieving families.
She stays **anxious** even with long warning because she distrusts official dates.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no slow corner left to move into.
whatWouldHelp: A **year's notice** from employers and help moving into **funeral work**.
